title: Retorsion: Rome's Scripture-plus-tradition rule fails the same self-witness test
source_text: XXX. Quod ut evidentius fiat, rogamus Pontificios, si Scriptura non sit integra & sufficiens fidei regula, dicant nobis quae tandem illa sit. Respondebunt regulam illam constare tam verbo scripto, quam non scripto, quod est in ore Ecclesiae Romanae: Et verbum illud tam scriptum, quam non scriptum esse sufficientem & totalem fidei regulam, extra quam non sit aliud Dei verbum, & ex qua sola peti possint ea quae sunt necessaria ad fidem & salutem. Sic vero jam proprium eorum argumentum in ipsos retorqueo. Verbum illud partim Scriptura sacra constans, partim sine scripto traditionibus quibus Ecclesia Romana testimonium perhibet, non est sufficiens fidei regula. Nec enim omnia quae sunt ad fidem necessaria ex eo probari possunt. Etenim omnium maxime necessarium est ut credamus esse aliquod verbum vere divinum, & verbum istud constare partim Scripturis quibusdam, partim non scriptis traditionibus, & divinas istas Scripturas atque traditiones esse illas ipsas quibus Ecclesia Romana testimonium perhibet; nosque posse ac debere testimonio ejus hac in parte credere, tanquam omnino certo atque infallibili. Sed istud dogma tam necessarium, & quod tanquam totius religionis fundamentum profertur, non potest sufficienter haberi ex verbo, seu scripto, seu non scripto, quod est in ore Ecclesiae Romanae. Nam quamvis Scriptura affirmet se divinitus inspiratam esse, & Ecclesia Romana glorietur traditiones suas esse divinas, & verbum Dei ab ipsa tanquam ab infallibili teste petendum esse, Nec Scripturae tamen, nec traditionibus, nec Ecclesiae Romanae certo credam, quin prius credam Deum per Romanam Ecclesiam loqui, & tam Scripturam quam traditiones a Deo suam ducere originem. Itaque necesse est, praeter Scripturam & traditiones, & ipsum Ecclesiae Romanae testimonium, esse quoddam Dei verbum unde discam ista omnia esse divina, & fidem meam obligare: alioqui fides mea de authoritate verbi tam scripti, quam non scripti quod in ore habet Ecclesia Romana, nullo nitetur Dei verbo, & sic non erit fides. Denique nulla fidei regula fingi potest contra quam aliquis non possit simili argumento uti.
pass_a_gloss: That this may become more evident, we ask the Pontiffs, if Scripture is not an entire and sufficient rule of faith, let them tell us what that rule finally is. They will answer that that rule consists both of the written word and of the unwritten, which is in the mouth of the Roman Church: And that that word, both written and unwritten, is a sufficient and total rule of faith, outside which there is no other word of God, and from which alone those things which are necessary to faith and salvation can be sought. But thus I already turn their own argument back upon them. That word consisting partly of sacred Scripture, partly of unwritten traditions to which the Roman Church bears testimony, is not a sufficient rule of faith. For not all things which are necessary to faith can be proved from it. For it is most necessary of all that we believe there is some truly divine word, and that that word consists partly of certain Scriptures, partly of unwritten traditions, and that those divine Scriptures and traditions are those very ones to which the Roman Church bears testimony; and that we can and ought to believe her testimony in this part as altogether certain and infallible. But that dogma so necessary, and which is brought forward as the foundation of the whole religion, cannot be sufficiently had from the word, whether written or unwritten, which is in the mouth of the Roman Church. For although Scripture affirms that it is divinely inspired, and the Roman Church boasts that her traditions are divine, and that the word of God is to be sought from her as from an infallible witness, yet I will not certainly believe either Scripture, or the traditions, or the Roman Church, unless I first believe that God speaks through the Roman Church, and that both Scripture and the traditions draw their origin from God. Therefore it is necessary that besides Scripture and the traditions, and the Roman Church's own testimony, there be some word of God from which I learn that all those things are divine and bind my faith: otherwise my faith concerning the authority of the word both written and unwritten which the Roman Church has in her mouth will rest on no word of God, and thus will not be faith. Finally no rule of faith can be imagined against which someone could not use a similar argument.
pass_b_english: Ask Rome: if Scripture is not the whole sufficient rule, what is?
They answer: written plus unwritten word in Rome's mouth — the total rule outside which there is no other word of God.
Retorsion: that mixed rule also cannot prove what is most necessary — that Rome's Scriptures and traditions are the divine ones, and that her witness is infallible.
Scripture's self-claim and Rome's boast do not settle the point until one already believes God speaks through Rome.
So their rule demands yet another word beyond Scripture, tradition, and Rome's testimony — or faith rests on no word of God.
No faith-rule escapes a similar charge.
